newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Some 1,700 soldiers in Albania as force grows.
newsitem.headline: Some 1,700 soldiers in Albania as force grows.

text.p: A multinational force arriving in Albania to secure humanitarian aid convoys will need about three weeks before it is fully operational, a spokesman for the Italian army, which is leading the mission, said on Thursday.

Colonel Gianfranco Scalas told a briefing the U.N.-backed mission, codenamed Alba (Dawn), had got off to a good start and about 1,700 soldiers in the force that will eventually number 6,000 had reached the violence-stricken Balkan state.
"We are very content with the start of the mission," said Scalas.

"It will take us some time to adapt ourselves to the conditions in Albania. We will need some time, perhaps three weeks, to adapt. We have to build camps, set up kitchens, canteens and toilet facilities."
Scalas said 700 Italian, 456 French, 350 Spanish, 120 Greek and 153 Turkish soldiers had reached Albania. Soldiers from Romania, Denmark and Austria were due within the next few days.
About 400 military vehicles, including tanks and armoured personnel carriers (APCs), had arrived through the western port of Durres and Tirana airport.
"We are moving at full speed and the figure for the number of arrived is changing every hour," he said.

The mission is to prepare the way for the arrival of badly needed aid to the impoverished country, which has been racked by violence and lawlessness since the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes earlier this year.
Some 300 people have been killed and 700 injured during the weeks of armed anarchy and banditry that have swept Europe's poorest nation.
Scalas said the Italian transport ship San Marco was due to bring in a mechanised brigade to Durres on Friday.

A small force of 25 Italian marines arrived by land in the southern rebel-held port of Vlore on Thursday. They were the first troops to reach the south since the multinational force landed in the chaotic Balkan state.
Vlore is the third key port of entry into Albania.
At a briefing in Rome, Admiral Guido Venturoni, Italy's Defence Chief of Staff, repeated that the force's mandate did not call for disarming Albanians.

"The mandate does not call for rounding-up operations or disarming. This is not part of the mandate," he told a questioner. "Naturally, if people with weapons threaten the force, the force will respond," he said.
He said the force's interlocutors on the ground would be "those indicated to us by the government. This is a government of national unity".
Italian defence officials said an Italian AMX jet would carry out reconnaissance missions over Albania.
Venturoni said the purpose of the AMX mission would be "to see to it that Albanian air installations are in safe hands".
Venturoni said he expected full contingents of Italian, Greek and Romanian soldiers to arrive in Vlore "in a matter of days".
The small Italian team already there was evaluating the conditions of the port and its security, he added.
Defence Ministry spokesman Colonel Mario Fatone said Slovenia, Belgium and the Netherlands had expressed interest in taking part in the force.
